body:
The Andaman volcanic region

The Andaman and Nicobar Islands lie near an active tectonic boundary associated with the northward continuation of the Sunda subduction system. Oceanic lithosphere of the Indian Plate descends beneath the Burma microplate region, creating conditions favourable for volcanic activity.

Barren Island and Narcondam Island are important volcanic islands associated with this tectonic setting.

Barren Island

Barren Island, situated in the Andaman Sea to the northeast of Port Blair, now officially named Sri Vijaya Puram, contains India's only historically active magmatic volcano.

The volcano is classified as a composite volcano or stratovolcano. It consists of a volcanic cone within a larger caldera and has produced both explosive activity and lava flows.

  • The earliest recorded eruption dates to 1787.
  • Renewed volcanic activity in 1991 marked its first recorded eruption of the 20th century.
  • During the 1991 eruption, lava reached the sea and generated steam where the hot lava encountered seawater.
  • Several subsequent eruptions have been documented.

Documented eruption record

The Smithsonian Institution's Global Volcanism Program lists a confirmed eruption of Barren Island from 30 July 2025 to 11 January 2026. Its database classified Barren Island as a stratovolcano and listed 2026 as the last known eruption year when consulted on 27 November 2026. This is a documented eruption record, not a real-time declaration of volcanic activity.

Narcondam Island

Narcondam is a volcanic island situated north-northeast of Barren Island in the Andaman Sea. It is classified as a stratovolcano but has no confirmed historically recorded eruption.

The absence of a confirmed historical eruption does not, by itself, establish that a volcano is permanently extinct. Barren Island and Narcondam should therefore be distinguished according to their documented eruption histories.

The mud volcanoes of Baratang

Baratang Island in the Andaman Islands is known for its mud volcanoes. These features discharge mud, water and gases under underground pressure.

Mud volcanism is different from ordinary magmatic volcanism because it does not require the eruption of molten silicate rock. An active mud volcano is therefore not equivalent to an active lava-producing volcano.

The Deccan Traps

The Deccan Traps constitute a major continental flood basalt province in western and central India. Their main volcanic phase occurred approximately 66 million years ago, near the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary.

Successive eruptions of highly fluid basaltic lava through fissures covered extensive regions. The resulting layers accumulated into a thick volcanic succession.

The name Traps refers to the characteristic staircase-like topography that develops through differential weathering and erosion of these lava layers.

The Deccan Traps are widely associated with ancient hotspot-related volcanism connected to the Réunion mantle hotspot. They represent the remnants of an ancient volcanic province rather than an active volcanic arc comparable to the Andaman region.

Volcanic geology of Gujarat

Deccan basalt occurs extensively in parts of Saurashtra and in parts of eastern and southern Gujarat. Ancient lava flows have contributed to the development of plateaus, stepped hills and other characteristic rock-controlled landforms.

  • Saurashtra: Extensive basaltic formations reflect ancient Deccan volcanic activity.
  • Eastern and southern Gujarat: Areas bordering the alluvial plains contain characteristic Deccan Trap topography.
  • Narmada valley: Geological formations include prominent intrusive dykes associated with the volcanic province.

Ancient volcanic rocks are important evidence of past geological processes, but their presence does not establish that a region is currently volcanically active.

Important Indian volcanic features compared

FeatureLocationDistinction
Barren IslandAndaman SeaHistorically active stratovolcano
NarcondamAndaman SeaNo confirmed historical eruption
BaratangAndaman IslandsMud volcanism
Deccan TrapsWestern and central IndiaAncient flood basalt province

Prelims focus

  • Barren Island is located in the Andaman Sea.
  • Barren Island's earliest recorded eruption dates to 1787.
  • Narcondam lies north-northeast of Barren Island.
  • Baratang is associated with mud volcanism.
  • The Deccan Traps formed principally around 66 million years ago.
  • Trap: Ancient basaltic rocks in Gujarat do not indicate present-day magmatic eruptions.

[References: Smithsonian Institution, Global Volcanism Program, Barren Island, volcano profile 260010, Eruptive History and August 1991 Bulletin; Global Volcanism Program, Narcondam volcano profile; Andaman and Nicobar Administration, Directorate of Tourism, Mud Volcano; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Deccan Traps at Panchgani and Mahabaleshwar; The Magmatic Architecture of Continental Flood Basalts I: Observations From the Deccan Traps, Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth, 2021; V. N. Kulkarni, Geology of Gujarat, Government of Gujarat, 1985, pp. 1–2 and Geological Formations. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

body:
Major volcanic hazards

Volcanic eruptions can affect areas close to the vent as well as distant regions. The nature of the hazard depends on eruption behaviour, volcanic products, topography, weather conditions and the distribution of settlements.

Lava flows

Lava flows consist of molten rock moving across the surface. They can bury agricultural land, destroy buildings, interrupt roads and damage utilities. Many lava flows advance relatively slowly compared with explosive volcanic currents, although their speed varies with lava properties and slope.

Pyroclastic density currents

A pyroclastic density current is a rapidly moving, ground-hugging mixture of hot volcanic gases and fragmented material. It may develop through the collapse of an eruption column, explosive activity or the collapse of unstable lava domes.

Pyroclastic currents are particularly dangerous because of their high temperatures, rapid movement and destructive force.

Volcanic ashfall

Explosive eruptions can inject fine volcanic particles into the atmosphere. Winds may transport this ash far from the volcano.

Ashfall can reduce visibility, irritate the respiratory system, contaminate water, damage crops and machinery, and overload roofs. Airborne volcanic ash is particularly hazardous to aircraft engines.

Lahars

A lahar is a flowing mixture of water and volcanic debris. Heavy rainfall, melting snow or ice, or the release of water from volcanic lakes can mobilise loose volcanic deposits.

Lahars may travel considerable distances along valleys and river channels. They can occur during eruptions or long after eruptive activity has ceased.

Volcanic gases

Volcanoes release gases including sulphur dioxide, carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulphide. Some gases are toxic or irritating, while others can accumulate in hazardous concentrations.

Carbon dioxide is denser than air under comparable conditions and can accumulate in poorly ventilated depressions. Sulphur dioxide can contribute to respiratory irritation and acidic atmospheric deposition.

Volcanic eruptions and climate

Large explosive eruptions can influence climate when substantial quantities of sulphur dioxide reach the stratosphere. Chemical reactions convert some of this gas into fine sulphate aerosol particles.

These particles reflect part of the incoming solar radiation, reducing the amount of solar energy reaching the lower atmosphere and surface. The resulting effect can be temporary regional or global cooling.

The climatic effect depends on eruption magnitude, sulphur emissions, injection altitude and atmospheric circulation. A large ash plume alone does not necessarily imply substantial long-term cooling because much volcanic ash settles out of the atmosphere relatively quickly.

Volcanoes also release carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas. Volcanism can therefore have different climatic effects depending on the gases emitted and the timescale considered.

Monitoring volcanic activity

Magma movement and pressure changes can produce measurable changes before some eruptions. Scientists monitor several indicators together to assess whether volcanic unrest is increasing.

Monitoring methodWhat it can indicate
Seismic monitoringRock fracturing, magma movement and volcanic tremor
Ground deformationInflation or subsidence associated with changes in underground pressure
Gas measurementsChanges in volcanic gas release and composition
Thermal monitoringChanges in surface temperature and heat emission
Satellite observationsThermal anomalies, ash plumes and ground deformation

Satellite observations are especially valuable at remote or difficult-to-access volcanoes, including isolated volcanic islands.

Increased seismicity, deformation or gas emissions may indicate volcanic unrest, but no single observation guarantees that an eruption will occur. Monitoring improves hazard assessment and eruption forecasting without providing perfect certainty.

Volcanic risk reduction

Volcanic hazard maps help identify areas potentially exposed to lava, pyroclastic currents, ashfall and lahars. Risk can be reduced by restricting development in highly hazardous areas, maintaining evacuation arrangements, issuing timely warnings and educating communities.

During ashfall, people should follow official advice on remaining indoors, protecting breathing and eyes, and avoiding unnecessary travel. In threatened valleys or areas exposed to pyroclastic currents and lahars, timely evacuation is particularly important.

Prelims focus

  • Pyroclastic currents contain hot gases and fragmented volcanic material.
  • Lahars contain water mixed with volcanic debris.
  • Volcanic ash presents a serious aviation hazard.
  • Stratospheric sulphate aerosols can produce temporary cooling.
  • Seismicity, deformation, gases and heat are major volcanic monitoring indicators.
  • Trap: Lahars can occur without an eruption taking place at that moment.

[References: US Geological Survey, Volcano Hazards Program, Volcanic Hazards, Volcanic Ash Impacts and Mitigation, Volcanoes Can Affect Climate and Monitoring Volcanoes; Smithsonian Institution, Global Volcanism Program, Barren Island, Weekly Volcanic Activity Report, 8–14 January 2026. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

body:
Volcanism as a constructive geological process

Although volcanic eruptions can be extremely destructive, volcanic processes also create land, rocks, soils and economically useful resources. Many productive agricultural regions and settlements have developed on landscapes formed by ancient volcanic activity.

Formation and fertility of volcanic soils

When lava, ash and other volcanic deposits undergo weathering, their mineral constituents gradually break down and contribute to soil formation.

Volcanic materials may supply important plant nutrients, including potassium, calcium and magnesium. Fine volcanic material can also develop favourable soil properties under suitable climatic and biological conditions.

However, fresh volcanic ash is not automatically fertile agricultural soil. Newly deposited ash may bury crops, damage vegetation or create unfavourable chemical conditions. The development of productive soil depends on weathering, organic matter accumulation, drainage, climate and the composition of the parent material.

Black soil and the Deccan volcanic region

The weathering of basaltic rocks has played an important role in the formation of the black soils found across large parts of the Deccan region. Black soil is commonly called regur soil or black cotton soil.

These soils are widespread in Maharashtra, parts of Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and other areas of the western and central Deccan region. In Gujarat, black soils occur extensively in parts of Saurashtra and in several southern and central agricultural regions.

Characteristics of black soil

  • Generally high clay content and considerable moisture-retaining capacity.
  • Expansion and stickiness when wet.
  • Shrinkage and the development of deep cracks during dry conditions.
  • Suitability for cotton cultivation, along with several other crops under appropriate conditions.

Black soil should not be treated as synonymous with every volcanic soil. Not all volcanic soils are black, and the properties of soils developed from volcanic rocks vary with environmental conditions.

Volcanic rocks and mineral resources

  • Construction materials: Basalt is widely used as crushed stone and aggregate. Other igneous rocks are used as building and decorative stone.
  • Pumice: A light, porous volcanic rock used in abrasives and some lightweight construction products.
  • Metallic minerals: Magmatic and associated hydrothermal processes can concentrate economically valuable minerals, including copper and gold.
  • Secondary minerals: Mineral-bearing fluids circulating through cavities and fractures in volcanic rocks may deposit useful or collectible minerals.

Hydrothermal processes involve the movement of hot, mineral-bearing water through rocks. As temperature, pressure or chemical conditions change, dissolved minerals may precipitate and accumulate in particular locations.

Geothermal energy

The Earth's internal heat can warm underground rocks and groundwater. In suitable geological settings, hot water or steam can be used directly for heating or to generate electricity.

Geothermal energy is particularly accessible in many volcanic and tectonically active regions because underground heat sources may occur relatively close to the surface.

Hot springs and geysers can form where groundwater is heated underground and returns to the surface. A geyser periodically ejects hot water and steam, whereas a hot spring usually discharges heated water more continuously.

Iceland provides an important example of the use of geothermal resources in a volcanic region. Geothermal resources can also occur in non-volcanic regions where underground geological conditions permit the circulation and heating of water.

Volcanism, earthquakes and their common geological origin

Earthquakes and volcanism both reflect the Earth's internal geological activity, but they are not identical processes. Earthquakes involve the release of energy through seismic waves, usually during fault movement. Volcanism involves the formation, movement and possible eruption of magma.

They commonly occur together at subduction zones because tectonic movement produces earthquakes while water released from descending plates promotes magma formation. Divergent boundaries also produce earthquakes and volcanism because separating plates generate fractures and encourage decompression melting.

Nevertheless, many tectonic earthquakes occur without volcanic eruptions. Large ancient volcanic provinces may also remain geologically inactive long after their original formation.

Integrated prelims distinctions

ConceptsEssential distinction
Focus and epicentreUnderground rupture origin and corresponding surface point
P-wave and S-waveCompressional wave and shear wave
Magnitude and intensitySource size and local shaking severity
Prediction and early warningFuture event specification and detection after an event begins
Magma and lavaUnderground molten material and erupted molten rock
Effusive and explosive eruptionLava outpouring and rapid fragmentation
Intrusive and extrusive bodiesSolidification below and at the surface
Earthquake and tsunamiSeismic ground motion and water waves produced by displacement

Prelims focus

  • Deccan basalt is an important parent material of black soil.
  • Regur soil retains moisture and develops cracks when dry.
  • Magmatic and hydrothermal processes can concentrate metallic minerals.
  • Geothermal energy utilises the Earth's internal heat.
  • Subduction zones commonly produce both earthquakes and volcanism.
  • Trap: Every volcanic deposit does not immediately form fertile soil.

[References: NCERT, Contemporary India II, Class 10, Chapter 1, Resources and Development, Black Soil, online textbook extract available through SATHEE, IIT Kanpur; NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, 2018–19 reprint, Chapter 2, Rocks and Minerals; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2026–27 reprint, Chapter 3; US Geological Survey, What Are Some Benefits of Volcanic Eruptions? and Volcanoes and People; NOAA JetStream, Plate Tectonics and Earthquakes; V. N. Kulkarni, Geology of Gujarat, Government of Gujarat, 1985. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]
